The diagram shown above is the slope field for which of the following differential equations?
worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14040443/assets/50b53f35a936263f72a3962e32d841dc85519fb5ef3e7e138111c4efeb38137e.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes of the slope field are horizontal along the lines $y=-1$ and $y=2.$ Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should equal zero on both of these lines.

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(y+1)(y-2)^{2} \\ {y}^{′} & =(y+1)(y-2) \\ {y}^{′} & =y(y+1)(2-y)\end{aligned}
$$

We can dismiss the equation ${y}^{′}=y(y+1)(2-y).$ Although the right-hand side evaluates to zero at $y=-1$ and $y=2,$ it also evaluates to zero when $y=0,$ which is behavior not exhibited by our slope field.

- Second, the lines $y=-1$ and $y=2$ divide the plane into $3$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $3$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| Region | $y<-1$ | $-1<y<2$ | $y>2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slope | $↘$ | $↗$ | $↗$ |
| Sign | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |

Of the remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}=(y+1)(y-2)^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${y}^{′}=(y+1)(y-2)^{2}.$
